lessons.title: Enter calculations accurately
lessons.summary: Copy the grouping of a written calculation into a scientific calculator and check the entry before finding its value.
lessons.objective: Copy the grouping of a written calculation into a scientific calculator and check the entry before finding its value.
lessons.before: Use the scientific calculator you know. Key names may differ between models.
lessons.ideas:
The fraction \(\dfrac{8+3}{9-4}\) has two grouped expressions. It is one division of the value on top by the value below.

Include every term beneath the bar in the same root. When you have copied all those terms, move the cursor out of the root or close its brackets.

In \((-6)^2\), the whole negative number is the base of the square. In \(-6^2\) the leading minus is outside the power.
lessons.method:
How do I keep a numerator and denominator together?

Use a fraction template if your model has one. Enter the top, move to the bottom and enter it. For a one-line entry, put brackets around each whole part and put division between them.

How far does the root extend?

Point to the first and last term under the written bar. Type those terms with their signs inside one root. Read the grouped entry back before evaluating.

When do I need brackets around a negative number?

Use the sign key or model equivalent to enter the negative number. Put brackets around the negative base before raising it to a power. Exit the power before typing the next operation.
mistakes: Typing a plus or minus after finishing a fraction changes which part it belongs to. Compare the expression on your screen with the original fraction bar.
If you leave the root too early, later terms are added or subtracted after the root has been calculated.
A subtraction sign typed in place of a negative sign can give a syntax error or change the entry. Check both the sign and the brackets.

examples.title: Keep both parts of a fraction together
examples.question: Use your calculator to find \(\frac{11+6}{9-3}\). Give the exact value.
examples.solution:
Put \(11+6\) in the numerator and \(9-3\) in the denominator. With a division key, enclose both parts in brackets.

The calculator is dividing \(17\) by \(6\). The exact answer is \(\frac{17}{6}\).

examples.title: Check where the square root ends
examples.question: Use your calculator to work out \(\sqrt{81+19}\).
examples.solution:
Enter \(81+19\) inside one root template. In a one-line entry use brackets to put both terms inside the root.

The whole quantity under the root is \(100\). Its square root is \(10\).

examples.title: Enter a negative base with brackets
examples.question: Use your calculator to work out \((-6)^2+6\).
examples.solution:
Enter the negative sign and \(6\) within brackets before you press the square key. The base is \(-6\).

The square is \(36\). Move out of the exponent or close the brackets before adding \(6\). This gives \(42\).

lessons.title: Read the display and check the mode
lessons.summary: Choose the requested exact or decimal answer and check the angle setting when a question uses degrees.
lessons.objective: Choose the requested exact or decimal answer and check the angle setting when a question uses degrees.
lessons.before: Use the scientific calculator you know. Key names may differ between models.
lessons.ideas:
An exact fraction keeps the full value. A decimal display for a recurring fraction has a limited number of places and normally shows an approximation.

Changing how the answer is displayed keeps the stored value. Some calculators can also limit the number of decimal places they show, so inspect the display before copying it.

Use degrees when the question uses degrees. The indicator may say DEG or D. RAD or R indicates radians.
lessons.method:
Which version of the result should I keep?

Use your model’s answer-format control to view a decimal when the question asks for one. Keep the exact fraction if the question asks for an exact answer. If the task asks for digits displayed, copy the display before rounding.

How do I change the display without changing the result?

If a fraction terminates as a decimal, choose the decimal display and read its digits. You can also divide the numerator by the denominator to find the decimal.

What setting matches an angle in degrees?

Look up the angle setting on your model. Choose the unit given in the question, then check the indicator on the screen. Angle setting and decimal format are separate controls.
mistakes: A decimal approximation can look close to the fraction. If the question asks for the exact value, write the fraction or another exact form.
Use the numerator first. Reversing the division gives the reciprocal of the original answer.
Changing the display to a fraction or decimal leaves the angle unit alone. Check the angle indicator directly.

examples.title: Choose the exact calculator result
examples.question:
The calculator can show \(\frac{15}{7}\) or the six-place display \(2.142857\). The question asks for an exact answer. Which result should you write?

  1. \(2.143\)
  2. \(\frac{7}{15}\)
  3. \(\frac{15}{7}\)
  4. \(2.142857\)
examples.solution:
The decimal form of this fraction continues. The six decimal places on the display omit later digits.

Use \(\frac{15}{7}\). It records the whole value exactly.

examples.title: Switch a result to decimal form
examples.question: Your calculator shows \(\frac{3}{25}\). Use its answer-format control or divide the numerator by the denominator. Give the exact decimal.
examples.solution:
Change the format of the stored fraction to decimal. The answer-format control may have a different name on your model.

The exact decimal is \(0.12\). Converting the display has kept the same value.

examples.title: Choose a setting for an angle in degrees
examples.question:
The question includes the angle \(35^\circ\). Your calculator shows RAD. Which change makes the angle entry match the question?

  1. Select degrees (DEG or D).
  2. Keep RAD and enter the same number.
  3. Switch the answer from a fraction to a decimal.
  4. Turn on a fixed number of decimal places.
examples.solution:
The degree sign beside \(35\) gives the unit. The calculator’s RAD setting expects angles measured in radians.

Change the angle unit to degrees and check the indicator. The keys or menus depend on the model.

lessons.title: Keep precision and check the result
lessons.summary: Use the full stored answer between steps, record the final result as requested, and catch a wrong-looking display.
lessons.objective: Use the full stored answer between steps, record the final result as requested, and catch a wrong-looking display.
lessons.before: Use the scientific calculator you know. Key names may differ between models.
lessons.ideas:
Enter the whole expression with the right grouping, or use the last-answer memory if your model has it. The label ANS is common.

Read the original unrounded result for your final rounding decision. If an earlier part asked for a rounded answer, use the full value again when a later part continues the calculation.

A positive number multiplied by a factor below one half must give less than half the original value. If you divided, multiply the quotient by the divisor to check that you recover the starting number.
lessons.method:
How can I keep all the digits between steps?

Write the expression you are calculating on paper. Use the exact stored result or the full grouped expression on the calculator. Round only the answer requested at the end.

Which digits belong in the final answer?

Keep your full result on the screen until you have checked how many places the question requests. Apply the stated rounding rule once, at the end.

How can I check a result that looks wrong?

Use a quick size or sign check first. If the result fails, inspect what you typed. Re-enter the calculation with the full brackets and use an inverse check when it is available.
mistakes: Copying back a rounded result can spread the error to the next calculation. Use the stored answer before you change it.
Two rounds can create a different final digit. Start from the full calculator result for the requested precision.
Typing the same mistaken entry twice can repeat the same mistake. Use a different check, such as the inverse operation.

examples.title: Keep the stored value between steps
examples.question: The first step is \(\frac{29}{8}\). Write down the result after multiplying that full value by \(11\). Give the exact value.
examples.solution:
The first result is \(3.625\). Carry the full value through by leaving the two steps in one expression or by using the stored last answer.

Multiply it by \(11\) to get \(39.875\).

examples.title: Use all displayed digits before rounding
examples.question: For \(\sqrt{290}\), the decimal display shows \(17.02938637\). The question asks for 3 decimal places. What value do you submit?
examples.solution:
Use the full displayed value \(17.02938637\) when deciding the last digit to write.

The requested final result is \(17.029\). Keep the full calculator value for any further calculation.

examples.title: Use a quick size check
examples.question:
You want to calculate \(24\times0.19\). The second factor is less than \(0.5\). Which displayed result is correct?

  1. \(24.19\)
  2. \(4.56\)
  3. \(45.6\)
  4. \(0.456\)
examples.solution:
The product must be less than half of \(24\), so it must be less than \(12\).

Re-enter the digits carefully. The exact product is \(4.56\).

lessons.title: Read money and time on a calculator
lessons.summary: Interpret decimal money and enter or read durations in decimal hours or a supported hours–minutes–seconds display.
lessons.objective: Interpret decimal money and enter or read durations in decimal hours or a supported hours–minutes–seconds display.
lessons.before: Use the scientific calculator you know. Key names may differ between models.
lessons.ideas:
\(6.7\) pounds is £6.70. The decimal part is seven tenths of a pound, which is seventy pence.

In \(2.45\) hours, the fractional part is \(0.45\) hour. Multiply by 60 to get \(27\) minutes.

To enter 4 hours 36 minutes, use \(4+\dfrac{36}{60}=4.6\) hours. Some models also support a sexagesimal entry, shown as \(4^\circ\,36'\,0''\) in a time calculation.
lessons.method:
How do I write a decimal result as money?

Read the whole pounds from before the point. Read the pence from the two places after it. Write the unit and use both pence digits.

How do decimal hours give minutes?

Separate out the whole hours. Multiply the decimal part by 60 to find the remaining minutes. Check that the minutes are fewer than 60.

How do I enter hours and minutes correctly?

For decimal entry, divide minutes by 60 and add the whole hours. If you use a sexagesimal key, follow your model’s instructions and check whether the display is currently in decimal hours or hours, minutes and seconds.
mistakes: A tenths digit represents tens of pence. For example, £6.07 names seven pence and gives a different amount from £6.70.
The digits to the right of the decimal point are parts of one hour. Copying them directly as minutes changes the duration.
A sexagesimal display uses symbols that can also appear for angles. Read those three groups as time only when the calculation is about a duration.

examples.title: Write the calculator result as money
examples.question:
The calculator shows \(19.7\) pounds. Which written amount correctly uses pounds and pence?

  1. £19.70
  2. £19.07
  3. £197.00
  4. £19.00
examples.solution:
The first digit after the point represents tenths of a pound. There are 70 pence in that part.

Write two digits for the pence, so \(19.7\) pounds is written £19.70.

examples.title: Read the minutes in a decimal-hour display
examples.question: The calculator shows a duration of \(6.30\) hours. It contains 6 whole hours and some minutes. How many minutes remain after the 6 whole hours?
examples.solution:
The decimal part is \(\frac{3}{10}\) of an hour.

Multiply that part by \(60\). The duration is 6 hours 18 minutes.

examples.title: Enter hours and minutes as a decimal
examples.question: A calculation needs a duration of 1 hours 51 minutes in decimal hours. What number should you enter?
examples.solution:
Write the minutes as \(\frac{51}{60}\) of an hour.

Add this to \(1\). Use \(1.85\) for the decimal-hour entry.
